673.title: The Sacred Heart
673.hook: a Friday feast: the heart of Christ as love made visible
673.tomorrow: The Birth of John the Baptist (24 June)
673.howItsDone: Catholics keep the solemnity of the Sacred Heart on the Friday after the second Sunday after Pentecost, usually in June; many homes display a Sacred Heart image, and some Catholics practice the First Friday devotion of receiving communion on the first Friday of each month.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Corpus Christi, the host carried through town. Your line was carried through the streets.

Above the door of an Irish farmhouse, on a kitchen wall in Manila, on a holy card tucked in a wallet: Jesus, looking straight out, pointing to his own chest, where a heart is shown outside his robe: wrapped in thorns, topped with flames and a small cross, sometimes with a wound in its side. To anyone who didn't grow up with it, a heart on fire, outside a body, can look strange. For the families who hang it, it's simply part of the house. On a Friday in June, the Church keeps its feast.
screen: `A PICTURE IN THE KITCHEN.` → `A HEART ON FIRE, OUTSIDE.` → `A FRIDAY IN JUNE.`

segments.voice: The heart in that picture starts in John's Gospel, at the cross, in the Douay-Rheims: "But one of the soldiers with a spear opened his side, and immediately there came out blood and water." Some early Christian writers saw in that open side the birth of the Church, its sacraments flowing out. Medieval saints, women and men, wrote about resting in the wounded heart of Christ. Centuries later, in a convent at Paray-le-Monial in France, a nun named Margaret Mary Alacoque reported a series of visions. In them, Jesus showed her his heart and complained, in her telling, that it had loved people so much and was repaid with coldness. Behold this heart, he said. He asked for a feast on the Friday after the octave of Corpus Christi, and for people to receive communion on the first Friday of each month. Her claims met real resistance at first. It took almost two centuries before Pope Pius IX, in 1856, put the feast on the calendar for the whole Church. Now it falls on the Friday after the second Sunday after Pentecost, which usually lands in June, and June became the month of the Sacred Heart. What's the picture saying? Catholics read it this way: God's love isn't only an idea. It has a body, a pulse, and wounds. In Matthew, when Jesus speaks of his own heart, he doesn't say mighty. He says, "learn of me, because I am meek, and humble of heart."
screen: `A SPEAR OPENS HIS SIDE.` · `MARGARET MARY AT PARAY-LE-MONIAL.` · `PIUS IX, 1856: THE WHOLE CHURCH.` · `LOVE WITH A PULSE AND WOUNDS.` · then, large: `I AM MEEK, AND HUMBLE OF HEART.`

segments.voice: Place one hand flat on your chest and wait until you can feel the beat, a rhythm going since before you were born, without your help. Keep your hand there and think of one person you love who is hard to love right now. If you pray, you can pray for them, or say Jesus's words, meek and humble of heart; if you don't, feel the beat and wish them well.
Sacred Heart. The heart of Jesus, honored as love made visible, wounded and burning. Its feast is a Friday in June, for the whole Church since 1856. Today's word.

674.title: The Birth of John the Baptist (24 June)
674.hook: with Jesus and Mary, one of only three births in the calendar
674.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Nativity of John the Baptist as a solemnity on 24 June; in parts of Europe and Latin America, Saint John's Eve is kept with bonfires and festivals, and clergy and religious pray his father's song, the Benedictus, every morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sacred Heart, wounded and burning. Your line was behold this heart.

Saints are almost always remembered on the day they died: the day of death is the birthday into heaven. But three people get a feast for the day they were born. Jesus, on Christmas. Mary, in September. And one more, today, the twenty-fourth of June, six months before Christmas, near the longest day of the year in the north. In parts of Europe people still light bonfires on the night before. The baby is John, who'd grow up to baptize in the Jordan, and his birth starts with a man who can't speak.
screen: `SAINTS: THE DAY THEY DIED.` → `ONLY THREE BIRTHS.` → `A FATHER WHO CAN'T SPEAK.`

segments.voice: Luke tells it. Zachary is an old priest, and his wife Elizabeth has never had children. While he's serving in the Temple, an angel tells him they'll have a son, and Zachary doubts it. So he's struck mute until the day it comes true. Months of silence. The baby is born, and on the eighth day the relatives gather for the circumcision and the naming. Everyone assumes he'll be called Zachary, after his father. Elizabeth says no, he'll be called John. They argue: nobody in your family has that name. So they turn to the father and make signs at him. And Zachary, in the Douay-Rheims, "demanding a writing table, he wrote, saying: John is his name." Instantly his tongue is loosed, and he starts praising God. The song he sings, the Benedictus, is the Gospel canticle of Morning Prayer in the Liturgy of the Hours. The name John comes from the Hebrew Yohanan, God has been gracious. Choosing it meant breaking with family custom to follow what had been given. And why late June? Luke says Elizabeth was six months along when the angel came to Mary, so the calendar puts John six months before Christmas. Saint Augustine noticed that after John's birth the days start to shorten, and after Christ's they start to lengthen. He heard in it John's own line, from the fourth Gospel: "He must increase: but I must decrease." A whole life pointing past itself, built into the sunlight.

segments.voice: Bring to mind, one at a time, the family you were born into: parents, brothers and sisters, grandparents, whoever was there at the start. For some that's warm, for some it's complicated, painful or unknown, and that's all right; just hold what's true. If you pray, you can pray for each of them by name; if you don't, wish each one peace, including anyone you've lost touch with.

Your line: his name is john. A father's tongue, loosed by writing a name. Until tomorrow.

675.title: Saints Peter and Paul (29 June)
675.hook: the fisherman and the tentmaker, the two pillars of Rome
675.howItsDone: Catholics keep the solemnity of Saints Peter and Paul on 29 June; in Rome it's a city holiday, and the pope blesses the pallium, a woolen band, for archbishops appointed during the year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the birth of John the Baptist and the name Yohanan. Your line was his name is john.

Two giant stone statues stand guard in front of Saint Peter's Basilica in Rome. On one side, Peter, holding keys. On the other, Paul, holding a sword. The Church gives them one feast together, on the twenty-ninth of June, which is a little funny, because they didn't always get along. One was a fisherman from Galilee. The other was an educated Pharisee from a city in what is now southern Turkey who made tents for a living. And once, in front of everyone, one of them told the other he was wrong.
screen: `KEYS AND A SWORD.` → `THE FISHERMAN AND THE TENTMAKER.` → `ONE FEAST FOR BOTH.`

segments.voice: Peter first. Simon, son of John, a fisherman, renamed by Jesus, in the Douay-Rheims: "thou art Peter; and upon this rock I will build my church." Petros, rock. The keys in his statue come from the next line, the keys of the kingdom. Catholics see in Peter the first of the popes, the bishop of Rome. He's also the one who sank in the water, who denied Jesus three times, and who was forgiven on a beach. Then Paul. Saul of Tarsus, who persecuted the first Christians until a light knocked him to the ground. Acts says he worked as a tentmaker, and in his letters he says he worked night and day while he preached, so as not to be a burden. Now the argument. In his letter to the Galatians, Paul tells how Peter came to Antioch and ate with Gentile Christians, then pulled back when some men came from James in Jerusalem. Paul writes: "I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed." The Church kept that letter in the Bible. Both men ended up in Rome, and tradition says both died there under the emperor Nero. Peter, the story goes, was crucified, and asked to be crucified upside down. Paul, a Roman citizen, was beheaded, which is why he holds a sword. In the second letter to Timothy, Paul says: "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith." Two pillars, the Church calls them. Different, sometimes at odds, holding up the same roof.

segments.voice: Picture Rome: the basilica over Peter's grave, the pope, the parishes, the people on buses and the poor sleeping near the colonnade. If you pray, you can pray for the pope and the people of Rome; if you don't, think of two people in your own life who don't always agree but hold something up together, and be grateful for both.

676.title: Saint Mary Magdalene (22 July)
676.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Mary Magdalene on 22 July, raised from a memorial in 2016; the Gospel at Mass is John's account of her meeting the risen Jesus in the garden and being sent to the disciples.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saints Peter and Paul, the fisherman and the tentmaker. Your line was two pillars.

Mary Magdalene, the repentant prostitute: that's the woman in a great many paintings, films and sermons, going back centuries. The Gospels never say it. Not once. What they do say about her is far more interesting, and in 2016 the Church did something about it. Pope Francis raised her day, the twenty-second of July, from a memorial to a feast, the same rank as the apostles. And the Vatican's decree gave her an old title: apostle of the apostles.
screen: `WHAT PEOPLE THINK THEY KNOW.` → `THE GOSPELS NEVER SAY IT.` → `2016: RAISED TO A FEAST.`

segments.voice: Here's what the Gospels actually say. Luke names her among the women who traveled with Jesus and supported his work from their own means, and says seven devils had gone out of her: some serious affliction, healed. Matthew, Mark and John name her at the cross, after the other disciples had scattered. And all four put her at the empty tomb on Easter morning. In John she's alone in the garden, weeping, and mistakes the risen Jesus for the gardener until he says one word: her name, Mary. Then he sends her. Go to my brethren. And John says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Mary Magdalen cometh, and telleth the disciples: I have seen the Lord, and these things he said to me." In John, the first person sent to announce the resurrection is a woman, and the people she's sent to are the apostles. That's where the title comes from: apostle means one who is sent. So where did the other story come from? In 591, in a homily, Pope Gregory the Great treated Mary Magdalene, the unnamed sinful woman who anoints Jesus in Luke, and Mary of Bethany as one person. That reading shaped Western art and preaching for centuries. The Eastern churches kept them as three women. After the Second Vatican Council, the Roman calendar quietly separated them again, and the Gospel for her day became the garden in John. Thomas Aquinas, long before, had already called her apostolorum apostola. The Church's own feast now tells her story the way the Gospels do.

segments.voice: Think back over the last week and find one piece of genuinely good news, yours or someone else's: a recovery, a kindness, a baby, a reconciliation, a small win. Hold it a moment, let yourself feel it, and picture who would be glad to hear it. If you pray, you can give thanks for it first.

677.title: Joachim and Anne (26 July)
677.hook: Mary's parents, and near their day the World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly
677.howItsDone: Catholics remember Saints Joachim and Anne on 26 July, and on the fourth Sunday of July keep the World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly, begun by Pope Francis in 2021; Saint Anne is honored at many shrines as a patron of grandmothers and mothers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saint Mary Magdalene, apostolorum apostola, the apostle to the apostles. Your line was she was sent.

Who taught you your first prayer? For a surprising number of people, the answer isn't a priest or a parent. It's a grandmother. A woman at a kitchen table with a rosary, or a grandfather who took you to Mass when nobody else would. Today the Church remembers a grandmother and grandfather, the parents of Mary and so the grandparents of Jesus. And here's the twist: the Bible never mentions them. Not their names, not a line.
screen: `WHO TAUGHT YOU TO PRAY?` → `JESUS'S GRANDPARENTS.` → `THE BIBLE NEVER NAMES THEM.`

segments.voice: Their names come from a second-century writing called the Protoevangelium of James. It isn't scripture, and the Church never made it so, but it was widely read, and its stories shaped Christian art for centuries. In it, Joachim and Anne are an older couple, faithful and childless, grieving. Joachim goes out into the wilderness to fast; Anne weeps in her garden. An angel comes to each, and they meet at the city gate, and a daughter is born: Mary. The story echoes the Bible's own childless couples, Abraham and Sarah, and especially Hannah in the book of Samuel. Anne is in fact Hannah's name, which means grace. The Church keeps their memorial together on the twenty-sixth of July, and treats the details as tradition, not history. But one thing is certain even if the names aren't: Mary was raised by someone, and the faith that Mary would one day teach her son came to her from them. Scripture does have old people who carry faith forward. In the Temple, Simeon holds the infant Jesus and says, in the Douay-Rheims, "Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace." Paul writes to Timothy about a faith "which also dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois, and thy mother Eunice." In 2021, Pope Francis began a World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly on the fourth Sunday of July, close to this feast. The old aren't the end of the story. Often they're how it got to you.

678.title: The Transfiguration (6 August)
678.hook: the light on the mountain in high summer
678.carry: it is good to be here
678.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of the Transfiguration on 6 August, hearing one of the Gospel accounts of Jesus shining on the mountain; the same Gospel is also read on the Second Sunday of Lent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joachim and Anne, and Hannah, the name behind Anne. Your line was the old carry the faith.

Some evenings in August the light does something strange. The sun drops low, the air goes gold, and an ordinary street, a parking lot, a friend's face across a table, suddenly looks lit from inside. People try to photograph it. Then it's gone, and it's just dusk. In the first week of August the Church remembers a moment like that, on a mountain, when three fishermen saw their teacher's face shine like the sun. And one of them, not knowing what to say, said something anyway.
screen: `AUGUST LIGHT.` → `LIT FROM INSIDE.` → `THREE FISHERMEN ON A MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: Matthew, Mark and Luke all tell it. Jesus takes Peter, James and John up a high mountain, apart. And there he's transfigured before them: his face shines like the sun, his clothes turn dazzling white. Moses and Elijah appear, often read as the Law and the Prophets, talking with him. Luke adds what they talked about: his departure, which he was about to accomplish in Jerusalem. Then Peter, who never could stay quiet, says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Lord, it is good for us to be here: if thou wilt, let us make here three tabernacles." Three tents. Let's stay. Mark adds, gently, that he didn't know what to say, because they were terrified. Then a bright cloud covers them, and a voice says: this is my beloved Son, hear ye him. When they look up, there's only Jesus. And they go back down the mountain. That's the shape of it. A moment of glory, and nobody gets to build a house there. The Gospels set it just after Jesus first tells them he will suffer and die, and some readers have heard it as a gift for the hard road ahead: a glimpse to remember on Good Friday. The Gospels never name the mountain. Tradition says Mount Tabor in Galilee, and a church stands there now. The feast is very old in the East, and in 1457 Pope Callixtus III extended it to the whole Western Church, on the sixth of August. The Greek verb Matthew uses is the root of our word metamorphosis.
screen: `HIS FACE SHONE LIKE THE SUN.` · `MOSES AND ELIJAH.` · `LET US MAKE THREE TENTS.` · `BACK DOWN THE MOUNTAIN.` · then, large: `LORD, IT IS GOOD FOR US TO BE HERE.`

segments.voice: Go to a window or outside if you can, near sunset or sunrise if possible, and pick one patch of sky or one wall the light falls on. Watch the color shift, a cloud move, a brightness fade or grow, without photographing it or trying to keep it. If you pray, you can say Peter's line once: it is good to be here.
The Transfiguration. Jesus shining on the mountain before Peter, James and John, with Moses and Elijah beside him. Its feast is the sixth of August. Today's word.
Your line: it is good to be here. Then, back down the mountain. Day six hundred seventy-eight, done.

679.title: The Assumption (15 August)
679.hook: Mary taken up; in many places a public holiday with processions
679.howItsDone: The Assumption on 15 August is a solemnity and, in many countries, a holy day of obligation; in much of Europe and Latin America it's a public holiday with processions carrying a statue of Mary, and in Poland and elsewhere herbs and flowers are blessed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Transfiguration, light on the mountain. Your line was it is good to be here.

On the fifteenth of August, much of southern Europe shuts down. In Italy it's Ferragosto, and the cities empty out for the beach. But in a village square in Sicily, or a coastal town in Portugal, a statue of Mary leaves the church on the shoulders of men in white shirts, under strings of lights, with a band playing and fireworks after dark. In Poland, people bring bunches of herbs and flowers to be blessed. It's high summer, and the feast is about the end of a life.
screen: `AUGUST FIFTEENTH.` → `A STATUE ON SHOULDERS.` → `HERBS AND FLOWERS BLESSED.`

segments.voice: Catholics believe that at the end of her earthly life, Mary was taken up, body and soul, into heavenly glory. Assumption is from the Latin assumere, to take up. Notice the verb: Jesus ascends, by his own power; Mary is assumed, taken up by God. The belief is very old. In the Christian East, the feast is called the Dormition, the falling asleep of Mary, kept on this same date. Stories circulated early about the apostles gathered at her deathbed, and an empty tomb. But the Bible says nothing about how Mary's life ended, and the Church doesn't pretend it does. Only in 1950 did Pope Pius XII formally define the Assumption as dogma, and he chose his words carefully: having completed the course of her earthly life. He did not say whether she died first. The Orthodox speak of her falling asleep; some Catholic theologians hold that she died; the definition leaves the question open. On the feast, the Church reads from Revelation, in the Douay-Rheims: "a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars." Why does it matter? Catholics read it as a promise about everyone: not just a soul surviving, but the whole person, body included, raised. She went first. And week ninety-seven closes: the Sacred Heart, John's birth, Peter and Paul, Mary Magdalene, Joachim and Anne, the Transfiguration, and now the Assumption.
screen: `ASSUMERE: TO TAKE UP.` · `IN THE EAST: THE DORMITION.` · `DEFINED IN 1950, CAREFULLY.` · `WHAT CHRISTIANS HOPE FOR ALL.` · then, large: `A WOMAN CLOTHED WITH THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Walk slowly, at a procession's pace, the way a village procession sets off at dusk: outside as the day cools if you can, through your home if you can't, or along an evening road in your mind. Think of someone you love who has died. If you pray, pray a Hail Mary as you walk, or pray for them; if you don't, carry their memory along with you.
The Assumption. Mary taken up, body and soul, into heavenly glory at the end of her earthly life. Defined in 1950; kept on the fifteenth of August. Today's word.
Your line: she went ahead. Where she went, Christians hope to follow. See you tomorrow.
